staged_source_snapshot.description: Stage 01 reproduced against this staged vulnerable checkout, and the line locations below match that workspace.

bug_description.original: OSS-Fuzz issue 42481865 (htslib): Heap-buffer-overflow READ {*} found by fuzz target hts_open_fuzzer [asan]. https://issues.oss-fuzz.com/issues/42481865
bug_description.original_source: sample_info.json / sanitizer_trace.txt / default_crash_trace.txt / reproduction_report.json / patch.diff / staged vulnerable source
bug_description.normalized: The staged 331-byte CRAM 2.0 witness contains a mapped-slice header whose payload at file offset 132 decodes to `ref_seq_id = 0`, `ref_seq_start = -1073213441`, `ref_seq_span = 36`, `ref_base_id = 0`, and a nonzero 16-byte MD5. Later, the external block header at file offset 263 decodes `content_id = 0` and `uncomp_size = 35`, and `cram_read_block()` allocates a 35-byte heap buffer for that block. In `cram_decode_slice()`, `cram_get_block_by_id()` selects that same block as the embedded reference and aliases it through `s->ref`. The decoder then sets `s->ref_start = s->hdr->ref_seq_start` and `s->ref_end = s->hdr->ref_seq_start + s->hdr->ref_seq_span - 1`, so the present size guard compares `s->ref_end - s->ref_start` against `b->uncomp_size`; because the same `ref_seq_start` appears on both sides of the subtraction, it cancels out and the guard effectively checks `36 - 1 > 35`, i.e. `35 > 35`, which does not reject the too-short block. In the MD5 path, `start = 0`, `len = 36`, the later `start + len > s->ref_end - s->ref_start + 1` clamp does not fire, and `hts_md5_update()` copies 36 bytes from the 35-byte buffer. AddressSanitizer reports the resulting heap-buffer-overflow read in `__asan_memcpy`. The saved patch instead rejects negative `ref_seq_start` / `ref_seq_span` earlier in `cram_decode_slice_header()`, which blocks this particular witness because its start is negative, but the load-bearing overread is admitted by the later off-by-one size check in `cram_decode_slice()`.

source.description: First project-code statement that materializes vulnerability-relevant mapped-slice header state from the attacker-controlled block bytes. The parsed `ref_seq_id` starts the header state that later selects the embedded-reference and MD5 path.
source.value_from: Static decoding of the staged `poc`'s mapped-slice block payload beginning at file offset 132 yields `ref_seq_id = 0`, then `ref_seq_start = -1073213441` from bytes `fc 00 80 ff ef`, `ref_seq_span = 36` from byte `24`, `ref_base_id = 0`, and a nonzero 16-byte MD5.
source.note: This is the earliest vulnerability-relevant parse step in project code for the crashing slice header.

sink.description: Closest project-level crash site. `hts_md5_update()` copies `size` bytes from `data`; here `data` still aliases the 35-byte embedded-reference block and `size` is 36, so the read crosses the heap allocation boundary.
sink.note: ASan reports `READ of size 36` in `__asan_memcpy`, and this final project `memcpy()` is the statement that performs that overread.

root_cause.description: Root cause. This guard validates the embedded-reference block using `s->ref_end - s->ref_start`, which equals `s->hdr->ref_seq_span - 1` because both ends are derived from the same `ref_seq_start`. The later MD5 path, however, uses the inclusive length `s->ref_end - s->ref_start + 1`. A 36-byte span against a 35-byte block therefore passes here and is later hashed as 36 bytes.
root_cause.note: The saved patch instead rejects negative `ref_seq_start` or `ref_seq_span` earlier in `cram_decode_slice_header()`. That blocks this exact witness because step 2 parsed a negative start, but the load-bearing overread on this path is admitted by the off-by-one size contract here.

tainted_value_origin.description: The attacker-controlled mapped-slice block payload is exposed as the parse pointer `cp`. The following ITF8 decodes and MD5 memcpy read directly from this buffer.
tainted_value_origin.note: For the crashing slice, this payload begins at file offset 132 in the staged `poc`.

parser_admitted.description: The input has already been admitted as CRAM and dispatched to a mapped-slice block; `cram_read_slice()` is now invoking the vulnerable slice-header parser on that block.

coarse_trace.summary: Reading the first CRAM record drives the CRAM backend into `cram_get_bam_seq()`, `cram_next_slice()`, and `cram_read_slice()`, which fetch the attacker-controlled slice header and data blocks.
The mapped-slice header bytes are parsed into `ref_seq_id = 0`, `ref_seq_start = -1073213441`, `ref_seq_span = 36`, `ref_base_id = 0`, and a nonzero MD5.
The external block later selected by `ref_base_id = 0` is decoded with `content_id = 0` and `uncomp_size = 35`, and `cram_read_block()` allocates a 35-byte heap buffer for it.

The decoder takes the embedded-reference path, aliases that 35-byte block as `s->ref`, and applies the guard `s->ref_end - s->ref_start > b->uncomp_size`; because this becomes `35 > 35`, the block passes and the later MD5 path requests 36 bytes.
The final `memcpy()` reads 36 bytes from the 35-byte embedded-reference block, matching the saved ASan heap-buffer-overflow.

fine_trace.note: Source. The mapped-slice header parser consumes attacker-controlled payload bytes beginning at file offset 132 and materializes `hdr->ref_seq_id = 0`. That nonnegative ID is the first header field that later steers the slice into mapped-reference handling.
The next ITF8 field becomes `hdr->ref_seq_start`. In the staged witness, bytes `fc 00 80 ff ef` decode to `-1073213441`, so the slice start is negative as soon as it is parsed.
The following ITF8 field becomes `hdr->ref_seq_span = 36` from byte `24`. This span later drives both the embedded-reference size check and the MD5 length.
Later in the same header block, the attacker-controlled reference-block selector is parsed as `hdr->ref_base_id = 0`. This value later chooses external block ID 0 as the embedded reference.
The parser copies 16 MD5 bytes from the attacker-controlled block. The staged witness supplies a nonzero value here, so the later `memcmp(..., 0, 16)` gate admits MD5 verification.

For the later-selected external block header at file offset 263, `cram_read_block()` decodes `content_id = 0` and `uncomp_size = 35` from bytes `00 04 00 23 23`. Because step 4 set `ref_base_id = 0`, this is the block whose size later feeds the embedded-reference guard.

The external block's heap buffer is allocated directly from `b->uncomp_size`. The saved ASan allocation stack lands on this exact line, so the selected embedded-reference block occupies a 35-byte heap region.
The decoded header state selects the embedded-reference arm. With `ref_id = 0` and `ref_base_id = 0`, the slice is treated as mapped and `embed_ref` becomes true.
`cram_get_block_by_id()` looks up block ID 0, uncompresses it if needed, and aliases its data as `s->ref`. This pointer now names the same 35-byte heap allocation from step 7.

Root cause. The decoder copies the same attacker-controlled start into `s->ref_start` and derives `s->ref_end = ref_seq_start + ref_seq_span - 1`. Because the same `ref_seq_start` appears on both sides of `s->ref_end - s->ref_start`, the guard effectively checks `ref_seq_span - 1 > b->uncomp_size`. With `ref_seq_span = 36` and `b->uncomp_size = 35`, it compares `35 > 35` and does not reject the too-short block.
The MD5 path derives the source offset into `s->ref`. Because `s->hdr->ref_seq_start` and `s->ref_start` are the same negative value, the `>=` arm is taken and `start` becomes `0`.
The MD5 path derives the hash length from the header span. Step 10 made `s->ref_end - s->ref_start + 1` equal to 36, so this condition is true and `len` becomes 36 from `s->hdr->ref_seq_span`.

fine_trace.code:
if (start + len > s->ref_end - s->ref_start + 1)
    len = s->ref_end - s->ref_start + 1 - start;
fine_trace.note: The final clamp does not reduce the MD5 length. With `start = 0`, `len = 36`, and `s->ref_end - s->ref_start + 1 = 36`, the predicate is false and `len` stays 36.
Inside the MD5-verification path, the decoder calls `hts_md5_update(md5, s->ref + 0, 36)` while `s->ref` still aliases the 35-byte embedded-reference block.

Sink. With `size = 36` and `data` still pointing at the 35-byte embedded-reference block, this `memcpy()` reads one byte past the heap allocation. The saved ASan report names the overread as `READ of size 36` in `__asan_memcpy`.

poc.trigger: The staged `poc` is a 331-byte CRAM 2.0 file. The mapped-slice payload at file offset 132 begins `00 fc 00 80 ff ef 24 ...`, which `cram_decode_slice_header()` parses as `ref_seq_id = 0`, `ref_seq_start = -1073213441`, `ref_seq_span = 36`, `ref_base_id = 0`, and a nonzero MD5. The external block header at file offset 263 begins `00 04 00 23 23`, which `cram_read_block()` decodes as `content_id = 0` and `uncomp_size = 35`. That exact header/block pairing drives `cram_decode_slice()` to hash 36 bytes from the 35-byte embedded-reference block.

format.contract: A 331-byte CRAM 2.0 file whose crashing slice header bytes at file offset 132 encode `ref_seq_id = 0`, `ref_seq_start = -1073213441`, `ref_seq_span = 36`, `ref_base_id = 0`, and a nonzero 16-byte MD5, and whose external block header at file offset 263 encodes `content_id = 0` and `uncomp_size = 35`. That exact pairing makes `cram_decode_slice()` call `hts_md5_update()` on 36 bytes of a 35-byte embedded-reference block.
